items.title: "AI is a technofascist, anti-human and anti-art project", says creator of lefty tech satire Future? No Thanks!, before explaining why he used it anyway
items.author: Edwin Evans-Thirlwell
items.summary: Prominent capital-p Political game developer and left-wing academic Paulo "Molleindustria" Pedercini has revealed that he used generative AI tools for aspects
items.text:
Prominent capital-p Political game developer and left-wing academic Paulo "Molleindustria" Pedercini has revealed that he used generative AI tools for aspects of recent ecosocialist satire Future? No Thanks!. According to Pedercini, "a tiny fraction of its code was written with AI support" towards the end of the project, specifically to assess and fix bugs.

The game also uses text-to-speech voice-acting for a couple of characters, generated with ElevenLab software, with Pedercini noting that the characters in question are intended as a spoof of wonky artificial intelligence. He insists that none of the game's art or writing is AI-generated. These insights arrive weeks after the game's Steam release, which was delayed due to Valve's concerns about sexual material. Back then, there was no genAI disclosure on the game's storepage. There is one now.

Pedercini fessed up about using generative AI on his blog yesterday. "Every independent gaming festival and showcase in the year 2026 requires some kind of generative AI disclosure," he begins. "That is great! Slop and vibe-coded games are a scourge, AI is a technofascist, anti-human and anti-art project, and it’s imperative to create spaces of resistance.

"Future? No Thanks! is a game that tackles the impact and limits of artificial intelligence head-on," Pedercini continues. "It satirizes generative AI and the careless ways it can be used, even in an enlightened ecosocialist world. It also dramatizes beneficial uses, such as coordinating a planned economy, voice recognition, and talking robots. And yet, I can’t say it’s a 100% AI free game."

In a breakdown of development of Future! No Thanks, stretching back to 2021, Pedercini comments that "99% of its code base was written before AI was even viable as a coding tool". As for why he decided to use it during the closing stages, he argues that "ChatGPT or Claude" can be "a powerful semantic search engine" when fixing bugs.

"Search engines have been enshittified to death, specific technical queries don’t yield meaningful results anymore," Pedercini writes. "Most search engines produce low quality AI responses anyway. Such coding assistance was used for things like fixing a shader I didn’t write which broke after an update, or diagnosing a one-frame loading glitch when loading sequences. Finishing touches and minor debugging.

"Unlike assets that can be easily swapped, AI generated code is hard to remove once introduced," he goes on. "I wouldn’t be able to tell which lines I wrote, which were generated, and which were somewhere in between."

Regarding the game's voicework, Pedercini argues that "text-to-speech used to be an uncontroversial technology and an early application of neural networks. Then the AI bros started commercializing AI voices as a way to replace human actors, so it’s now problematic."

Apparently, Future? No Thanks! features "about two minutes" of generated voicework "for an automated toilet and a personal assistant that mis-translates Roman idioms". Pedercini spells out that "the humor of these scenes relies on uncanny voices doing their job poorly". The Future? No Thanks! team experimented with human voices for these roles, he adds, but found "they just weren’t working as well". He includes a clip of the PA character for reference.

Watch on YouTube

Early demos of the game also featured some AI-generated "fake doo-woop tunes" with "AI" in the lyrics that "were supposed to make fun of losers who listen to slop". The referencing of AI in the lyrics was "conceived as a kind of mandatory watermark this future society imposes to AI-generated music," Pedercini explains. "I thought they were hilarious, but over time the association with a plagiarist tech company started to bother me so I replaced them with royalty free loops. By the way, royalty free samples that are certainly AI-free are increasingly hard to find, but I found an old site untouched since 2016."

Pedercini ends his blog (as of writing, anyway) with some thoughts on discussion around generative AI in games, commenting that the "100% no-AI stance/requirement" adopted by a fair few devs and players "is very recent, and the game was being developed before a consensus emerged". He adds that "as an educator I have to look into these tools which most of my students use, and I was trying to figure out if there are non-brain-rotting ways to do so. I’m grateful to those who allow some nuance in approaching the issue, especially regarding coding."

An older version of the blog had some lengthier thoughts about genAI, in which Pedercini argued that being "AI-free" is "the only truly ethical position" for game developers, given the technology's association with "energy and water use, IP theft, cheating, unemployment, spam, and so on". Nonetheless, he contended that genAI's evils reflect larger structural problems that can't be remedied through individual action, while arguing that "holding your fellow artists to the highest ethical standards won't stop the actual bad actors", and that enforcing "AI-free" within a "progressively minded community" may come at "a high cost of division, suspicion, and bad vibes".

These closing thoughts have now been deleted following some vehement responses on Bluesky, with Pedercini now commenting that they "made people upset and made me a strawman for arguments and positions I abhor". You can still find screen caps of the removed paragraphs in the wilds.

I like what I've played of Future! No Thanks?, and this is obviously a more "nuanced" injection of stochastic parrotry than the bazillions of quick cash-in games that consist purely of 'human-reviewed' generated code, or the blockbuster projects that are jamming it in at the behest of investors and executives. I broadly agree with Pedercini that generative AI is just the freshest wart on the arse of a callous social order that puts economic growth above everything else. I respect the intention to use the technology in the service of a story or theme, and I hear the point about certain, hitherto less damaging machine learning technologies being absorbed into the genAI crusade. And sure, people do like to tell each other off on social media, don't they?

That said, I find all this pretty disappointing. Given Pedercini's clear understanding of all the problems with generative AI, and given that Future? No Thanks! itself offers criticism of the tech, the least you'd expect is that he'd make his case for using the stuff in advance of selling the game. It would be a show of good faith. Pedercini also doesn't specify whether he sought out genAI tools that aren't as steeped in infamy as Claude, ChatGPT and Suno.

While I don't want to lean too much on commentary that has now been withdrawn, I also think Pedercini sets up too hard a binary between "individual action" and "structural problems" in the older version of the post. I agree that harping about "personal responsibility" is one of the weapons capitalism deploys to pit its discontents against each other, but a community that wants to create "spaces of resistance" against "a technofascist, anti-human and anti-art project" needs to hold members to an appropriate standard.

A number of other devs have responded to Pedercini's blog, including Necrobarista and Eternal Strands writer Damon Reece and Riot Games IP creative adviser Dante Douglas, who is also narrative lead on Airborne Empire. I imagine Pedercini will have more to say soon.

items.title: Endless pile of Needle In Haystack games begins to emerge, as viral hit imitator's devs claim their code was nicked by a genAI-using clone
items.author: Mark Warren
items.summary: In a metaphor far too on the nose to turn into any form of fiction, at least without the writer getting mercilessly cyberbullied, a game about finding a needle
items.text:
In a metaphor far too on the nose to turn into any form of fiction, at least without the writer getting mercilessly cyberbullied, a game about finding a needle in a haystack has now become the genuine needle at the heart of a pile of imitators. A pile so large, in fact, one copycat game stands accused of ripping code from another.

NoGlyph, developers of Needle In A Haystack, have claimed that their code's been nicked by A Game About Needle In A Haystack devs Little Field Studios. The former game was released on September 29th this year. The latter came out on October 16th. Both offer players a chance to go hunting for metal implements in piles of horse food, and both appear to have been inspired by the as-yet unreleased Needle In A Haystack Simulator, which gained notoriety after serving as the basis of a viral tweet in August.

These are just three of the needle-in-haystack games which've massed on Steam since that clip got a bunch of eyeballs, as various people look to fill the world's apparent desire to hunt stiching implements on a farm.

"Yesterday, on October 16th a game called 'A Game About Needle In A Haystack' by Little Field Studios came out on Steam," a Needle In A Haystack dev called Jahvin wrote in a Steam post over the weekend. "It contains code copied from our game. To be clear, this is about our actual code, not a similar idea or similar mechanics.

"The haystack in our game, meaning how it's drawn, how you dig into it and how gold, lapis and diamond hay work, is something that took a long time to get working properly. When we looked through their game's files, we found 13 of our classes inside it with the exact same names. More than half of the functions in that part match ours exactly. Some of our own error messages are still in there word for word, including one that points to a shader from our project that doesn't exist in their game.

"The copied code matches the versions of our free demo we put out on September 20 and 21, a few weeks before their release. From what we can tell, the rest of their game (the art, the sounds, the other systems) is their own work. Our problem is the hay code."

So, not an apparent copycat calling out another apparent copycat solely for its premise, but an accusation that things have evolved to the point of a studio directly ripping specific code and assets. The Needle In A Haystack devs added that they've filed a copyright notice with Valve and saved off a copy of their findings as proof.

A Game About Needle In A Haystack, the accused, boasts a genAI disclosure in its Steam description, but this only makes clear that the tech was used to produce the game's logo. If the hay code situation is as Jahvin described, that could suggest the potential for AI-assisted decompilation to have been at play in the alleged copying, but there doesn't seem to be any definite confirmation of that as of writing.

Dev concerns about AI being used to easily replicate games have been on the rise, following the recent boom in genAI-assisted decompilation. Just last week, the makers of a game called Drunken Goddess Reflux announced they'd cancelled plans for a public demo in favour of limited-access playtesting sessions, citing concern that "the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools, and that such works could be released before our launch".

Honestly, I'm just terrified that the ever-growing mound of needle-in-haystack variants will eventually grow to the point of causing Steam's vast barn of games to burst, sending horse-shaped westerns, pitchfork-shaped fantasy RPGs, and water trough-shaped games aimed at thirsty horndogs flying across the plains of the net.

NoGlyph, developers of Needle In A Haystack, have claimed that their code's been nicked by A Game About Needle In A Haystack devs Little Field Studios. The former game was released on September 29th this year. The latter came out on October 16th. Both offer players a chance to go hunting for metal implements in piles of horse food, and both appear to have been inspired by the as-yet unreleased Needle In A Haystack Simulator, which gained notoriety after serving as the basis of a viral tweet in August.

These are just three of the needle-in-haystack games which've massed on Steam since that clip got a bunch of eyeballs, as various people look to fill the world's apparent desire to hunt stiching implements on a farm.

"Yesterday, on October 16th a game called 'A Game About Needle In A Haystack' by Little Field Studios came out on Steam," a Needle In A Haystack dev called Jahvin wrote in a Steam post over the weekend. "It contains code copied from our game. To be clear, this is about our actual code, not a similar idea or similar mechanics.

"The haystack in our game, meaning how it's drawn, how you dig into it and how gold, lapis and diamond hay work, is something that took a long time to get working properly. When we looked through their game's files, we found 13 of our classes inside it with the exact same names. More than half of the functions in that part match ours exactly. Some of our own error messages are still in there word for word, including one that points to a shader from our project that doesn't exist in their game.

"The copied code matches the versions of our free demo we put out on September 20 and 21, a few weeks before their release. From what we can tell, the rest of their game (the art, the sounds, the other systems) is their own work. Our problem is the hay code."

So, not an apparent copycat calling out another apparent copycat solely for its premise, but an accusation that things have evolved to the point of a studio directly ripping specific code and assets. The Needle In A Haystack devs added that they've filed a copyright notice with Valve and saved off a copy of their findings as proof.

A Game About Needle In A Haystack, the accused, boasts a genAI disclosure in its Steam description, but this only makes clear that the tech was used to produce the game's logo. If the hay code situation is as Jahvin described, that could suggest the potential for AI-assisted decompilation to have been at play in the alleged copying, but there doesn't seem to be any definite confirmation of that as of writing.

Dev concerns about AI being used to easily replicate games have been on the rise, following the recent boom in genAI-assisted decompilation. Just last week, the makers of a game called Drunken Goddess Reflux announced they'd cancelled plans for a public demo in favour of limited-access playtesting sessions, citing concern that "the demo's content could be used to quickly imitate or replicate the game's presentation and gameplay with AI or other tools, and that such works could be released before our launch".

Honestly, I'm just terrified that the ever-growing mound of needle-in-haystack variants will eventually grow to the point of causing Steam's vast barn of games to burst, sending horse-shaped westerns, pitchfork-shaped fantasy RPGs, and water trough-shaped games aimed at thirsty horndogs flying across the plains of the net.

items.author: Clint Worthington
items.summary: Of the universe of Taylor Sheridan AARP-for-aging-’80s-guys dramas aimed squarely at the silent majority, “Tulsa King” is by far the most charming. Flitting
items.text:
Of the universe of Taylor Sheridan AARP-for-aging-’80s-guys dramas aimed squarely at the silent majority, “Tulsa King” is by far the most charming. Flitting somewhere between “Yellowstone” and “Get Shorty” in its tale of a New York goombah (Sylvester Stallone) starting his criminal enterprise all over again in Oklahoma, the show has spent three seasons simply letting its bulging cast of characters engage in soap-opera theatrics, squaring off against rival gang members and, in this last set of episodes, a vindictive bourbon distiller played by Robert Patrick. (Spoiler alert: Sly burns him at the stake in the season finale. I guess it’s the only way to be sure with the T-1000.) But in season four, “Tulsa King” finally feels like it’s getting lost in the literal and metaphorical sauce.

After taking over Patrick’s distillery, Dwight “The General” Manfredi (Stallone) is finally ready to legitimize his enterprises (well, some of them) and settle down with his girlfriend of three seasons, Margaret Devereaux (Dana Delany). Unfortunately, mysterious circumstances arise at the end of the season premiere that leave Dwight in deep mourning and unsure where his businesses stand with the government. That latter concern is compounded by the elevation of lieutenant governor Amanda Clark (Gretchen Mol), a by-the-books do-gooder who knows Dwight’s game and wants to shut him down permanently, to the top office.

That’s not Dwight’s only concern, of course; his old mafia family in New York City keeps gunning for the profits he’s been building in the Southwest, especially now that his old nemesis, Quiet Ray (James Russo), is fully in charge. What’s more, a greedy German AI tech bro (Flula Borg) is threatening to take Margaret’s horse ranch by eminent domain to turn the land into a data center.

(L-R): Scarlet Stallone as Spencer, Martin Starr as Bodhi, and Jay Will as Tyson in Tulsa King, episode 1, season 4, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. Photo Credit: Steve Swisher/Paramount+

All these conflicts and more stud “Tulsa King”‘s new season, and that’s not even getting into Bodhi’s (Martin Starr) flirtation with wine forgery, or Tyson’s (Jay Will) burgeoning rap career. And let’s not forget Dwight’s unsteady alliance with government spook Musso (Kevin Pollak) from last season and how that dovetails with Dwight’s existing animus with fellow capo Bevilaqua (Frank Grillo). Hey, there are a lot of aging character actors to pay; we gotta give them something to do, right? We should be thankful Samuel L. Jackson isn’t here to soak up more screen time, as he’s supposedly off building his own spinoff down in New Orleans.

“Tulsa King,” at this point, is more overstuffed than a turducken, with a cast so bloated that the gang is juggling at least three or four different schemes at once. Even Sly is getting a little tired; sure, some of that is Dwight’s puffed-up grief, but some of it is the older actor slowing down. (The show even writes a cane into Dwight’s ensemble; it’s passed off as an occasional knee injury that flares up from time to time, but I get the feeling that cane’s here to stay.) Even Sly coasting is compelling enough to watch, but you can tell the rest of the cast has to shore up their game to help carry this thing. This is especially true of Annabella Sciorra’s Joanne, Dwight’s enterprising sister and partner in crime, who slowly becomes the show’s heart and soul.

Gretchen Mol as Amanda Clark in Tulsa King, season 4, streaming on Paramount+, 2026. Photo Credit: Steve Swisher/Paramount+

In fact, you get the most enjoyment from showrunner Dave Erickson and his writing team’s occasional lapses into the ridiculous. Italian enforcer pals Goodie (Chris Caldovino) and Vince (Vincent Piazza) shoot their way out of a white supremacist meeting at a restaurant they happen to be eating at; “You just got robbed by two swarthy Mediterraneans!” they shout as they leave. Dwight mournfully asks an AI chatbot whether God exists, and the scene is treated as if it’s dispensing therapeutic wisdom from on high. Someone gets their head crushed in the jaws of a fossilized dinosaur skull. In these scenes, “Tulsa King” ekes out a kind of campy enjoyment. It’s just a shame you have to sift through so many diluted storylines to get there. (The less said about the budding romance between Garrett Hedlund’s Mitch and Scarlet Stallone’s Spencer, the better.)

It’d be dishonest to claim “Tulsa King” doesn’t offer consistent diversion, even amid the myriad components of Dwight’s business empire and all the spinning plates therein. But this season’s villains don’t compel (including everyone’s favorite “My Son Hunter” director Robert Davi as a creaky enforcer who looks like he can barely stand, let alone take out fools), and so many of the plot threads feel like filler to give Dwight’s bloated entourage things to do. The bulk of the show’s charm falls squarely on Stallone’s broad shoulders, and even he’s starting to lose a step. Here’s hoping the show can get its affairs in order in an already-announced season five, or this vital leg of the Taylor Sheridan universe will go, well, the way of the dinosaur.

Full season screened for review. Premieres October 16th on Paramount+.

items.text:
PlayStation Plus Free Games Lineup For November 2026 Is Off To A Rough Start

Published Oct 22, 2026, 5:56 AM EDT

James is a gaming writer from London who has spent thousands of hours exploring titles from every genre. Though he has a particular affinity for multiplayer titles like World of Warcraft, Destiny 2 and League of Legends, he has also put thousands of hours into single-player experiences, from deep RPGs to epic PC strategies. When he's not playing or writing, he can usually be found supporting his beloved Brentford FC.

Sony is going through a period of pretty unprecedented unpopularity right now, after their decision to move away from physical media drew the understandable ire of fans, both old and new. That controversy isn't going to go away any time soon either, unless the unlikely scenario of the company reversing its decision comes about at some point.

That said, the PlayStation remains the only console that a lot of players have access to right now, particularly with just how much new ones cost in light of the hardware crisis. If you are still maining the console, you likely also take advantage of PlayStation Plus, which brings monthly free games to players at no cost beyond their subscription.

Now, we're starting to learn about what November is going to look like for the service, and it's off to a less than encouraging start that won't fill large portions of the community with joy.

Rockstar Games

One of the most galling things about PlayStation Plus (and other equivalent services) is that, while we obviously get new games to play every month, we also lose games that fall by the wayside at the same time. November is no exception, and we're losing a lot of titles that fans will have been actively playing.

Over on Reddit, one user shared a list of games that are departing in November, and there were all sorts of comments from fans encouraging others towards specific titles, before they go away.

"I started playing Hotshot Racing yesterday and it's been a great dopamine rush so far. If you liked Outrun, you'll enjoy this too," one comment read.

While another added, "Talos 2 my beloved. Play it while you can, although the DLCs are great, so you may just want to buy the game. Up to you guys, but definitely try it."

A third was upset at Red Dead Redemption 2 cycling in and out so regularly, saying, "What's even the point of adding and removing RDR2 every few f**king months? It's a nearly 10 y/o game which doesn't have a PS5 port."

The full list of games that will be leaving PlayStation Plus in November is as follows:

Football Manager 2026

The Talos Principle 2

Red Dead Redemption 2

Grand Theft Auto V

Cricket 24

Monster Boy and the Cursed Kingdom

Hotshot Racing (Big Boss Bundle)

Rock of Ages III: Make & Break

Earth Defense Force 4.1 - The Shadow of New Despair

Rapala Fishing Pro Series

Yet Another Zombie Defense HD

It's undoubtedly a longer list than we get in a lot of months, but plenty of the titles are what we would consider more niche right now. The removal of GTA V is likely being done to accommodate the arrival of the next game in the series next month, while RDR2's constant cycling in and out of the system is being done to incentivize purchases. All in all, though, it's a rough start for PlayStation Plus next month, and there will need to be some solid additions to get things back in an overall positive place.

items.text:
Following EA's decision to shut down BioWare, the game that would've been the fifth entry in the Mass Effect series is being dumped out of an airlock, never to become a finished article that'll reach players hands as its creators envisioned. The larger tragedy is, of course, the job losses and the closure of a studio with a legacy befotting RPG royalty, but it's still sad that next Mass Effect will never come out, and some of the folks who worked on it have begun offering some insight into what the team were hoping to accomplish.

"I was one of the lucky ones who stayed with BioWare to start on the next Mass Effect, where I believe we were making something special: a level of autonomy and choice that no other game has been able to match," cinematic supervisor Tony de Waal wrote in a LinkedIn post revealing one of the 50 or so remaining BioWare staff let go as part of the closure. "We saw what Larian and CD Projekt were bringing to the table with their latest offerings, and started down a path to bring Mass Effect to the next level while remaining true to the Trilogy.

"I'm sad you won't ever get to see what we were cooking, and sad for the small, talented group of devs who were all punching above their weight to make something special. Please consider those who stayed with BioWare until the very end. They are truly some of the most talented people I've had the pleasure of working with throughout my career."

Writers Catherynne M. Valente and Derek Künsken didn't go into as much depth in their own posts on Twitter, but similarly echoed that they were excited about what the studio were sketching out and building with this Mass Effect game.

While it's worth maintaining the perspective that Mass Effect 5 was still early in development rather than minutes from being out of the door, it's galling that BioWare will never even get a chance to see if their plans could make for an RPG capable of pushing the genre forwards as the likes of Baldur's Gate 3, Cyberpunk 2077, and The Witcher 3 have over the past decade. Similarly to some of their long-established RPG-making cousins, the likes of Bethesda, BioWare's path hasn't been a straight line to massive success in recent years.

2017's Mass Effect: Andromeda wasn't as critically acclaimed and near-universally beloved as the trilogy that preceded it. Anthem failed to stick the live-service landing despite some promising ideas. Then, there was Dragon Age: The Veilguard, which had a well-documentedly messy development cycle that saw it pulled and pushed between multiplayer and singleplayer to suit the whims of EA management. The game it eventually turned into is one Nic (RPS in peace) summed up in his review as "a reluctant RPG, but a compelling, heartfelt action adventure". Sadly, it didn't sell the oodles of copies a game must to be deemed a success under EA these days, and thus seemed to instantly become the final black mark against BioWare that saw their corporate overlords start to fatally close in the walls.

Could BioWare have gotten their RPG master mojo back in full if they'd achieved their aims with Mass Effect 5? We'll never know. games studios under big publishers these days are rarely afforded such chances these days, no matter how obvious it might seem to those of us not just concerned with achieving short-term financial gains to offset being loaded up with debt in a Saudi-lead takeover by ditching everything that isn't turning over EA FC-level amounts of cash.

Matt Damon’s Pandemic Thriller Officially Becomes a Global Hit on HBO Max

Image via Roger Wong/INSTARimages

Published Oct 22, 2026, 5:00 AM EDT

Shrishty is a decade-old journalist covering a variety of beats between politics to pop culture, but movies are her first love, which led her to study Film and TV Development at UCLAx. She lives and breathes cinema and sometimes wakes up with the close-up shot of Ryan Gosling's hands playing piano in La La Land, in her head.
She has worked with numerous media outlets, including Burda Media (MSN News), DKODING Media, The Voice of Fashion, Hindustan Times, and more. Throughout her career, she has interviewed an array of people, from CEOs and politicians to filmmakers and farmers.

Timelessness makes a movie a classic; some are instantly deemed a force of nature, like Citizen Kane, The Wizard of Oz, The Godfather, and more. And then there are movies that earn "classic" status over time, like The Shawshank Redemption, Blade Runner, which audiences initially pannedbut built a massive underground sci-fi cult following on home video, or The Coen brothers’ The Big Lebowski, which got its due years later.

Another movie that fits the latter description is Steven Soderbergh’s Contagion, which, for good reason, became a pandemic-era watch as the world tried to make sense of its present. The thriller has a simple premise; Beth Emhoff (Gwyneth Paltrow) returns to Minneapolis from a business trip in Hong Kong and dies from a mysterious illness. Her husband, Mitch (Matt Damon), discovers he is naturally immune but must isolate to protect his daughter. Things take a turn when the mysterious illness becomes a pandemic, and an international team of doctors, coordinated by the World Health Organization (WHO), must deal with the rapid spread of a deadly virus.

In a curious case of life imitating art, the movie touches on the effects of globalization, where travel, urban density, and international commerce can turn a localized virus into a global catastrophe within days. It also addresses misinformation, as Soderbergh shows how panic and conspiracy theories spread faster than the virus itself. But the most chilling reflection comes from the film's examination of society's fragile veneer under martial law, juxtaposed with the self-sacrifice of public health workers. Remember that the feature came out in 2011, a decade before the real world saw a pandemic.

With compelling performers like Damon, Laurence Fishburne, Jude Law, Kate Winslet, Marion Cotillard, and Gwyneth Paltrow, Contagion became a worldwide hit, earning $136.5 million at the box office. The film was praised for Soderbergh’s detached direction, clinical accuracy, and its tense, documentary-like pacing. Nonetheless, it rose to modern-classic status during the pandemic, as people saw real life play out in real time, making its legacy almost prophetic.

Timelessness makes a movie a classic; some are instantly deemed a force of nature, like Citizen Kane, The Wizard of Oz, The Godfather, and more. And then there are movies that earn "classic" status over time, like The Shawshank Redemption, Blade Runner, which audiences initially pannedbut built a massive underground sci-fi cult following on home video, or The Coen brothers’ The Big Lebowski, which got its due years later.

Another movie that fits the latter description is Steven Soderbergh’s Contagion, which, for good reason, became a pandemic-era watch as the world tried to make sense of its present. The thriller has a simple premise; Beth Emhoff (Gwyneth Paltrow) returns to Minneapolis from a business trip in Hong Kong and dies from a mysterious illness. Her husband, Mitch (Matt Damon), discovers he is naturally immune but must isolate to protect his daughter. Things take a turn when the mysterious illness becomes a pandemic, and an international team of doctors, coordinated by the World Health Organization (WHO), must deal with the rapid spread of a deadly virus.
https://static0.colliderimages.com/wordpress%2Fwp-content%2Fauthors%2F68ac494d4f654-shrish%201_1.jpg?fit=crop&w=90&h=90

In a curious case of life imitating art, the movie touches on the effects of globalization, where travel, urban density, and international commerce can turn a localized virus into a global catastrophe within days. It also addresses misinformation, as Soderbergh shows how panic and conspiracy theories spread faster than the virus itself. But the most chilling reflection comes from the film's examination of society's fragile veneer under martial law, juxtaposed with the self-sacrifice of public health workers. Remember that the feature came out in 2011, a decade before the real world saw a pandemic.

With compelling performers like Damon, Laurence Fishburne, Jude Law, Kate Winslet, Marion Cotillard, and Gwyneth Paltrow, Contagion became a worldwide hit, earning $136.5 million at the box office. The film was praised for Soderbergh’s detached direction, clinical accuracy, and its tense, documentary-like pacing. Nonetheless, it rose to modern-classic status during the pandemic, as people saw real life play out in real time, making its legacy almost prophetic.

Dhruv is a Lead Writer in Screen Rant's New TV division. He has been consistently contributing to the website for over two years and has written thousands of articles covering streaming trends, movie/TV analysis, and pop culture breakdowns.
Before Screen Rant, he was a Senior Writer for The Cinemaholic, covering everything from anime to television, from reality TV to movies.
After high school, he was on his way to become a Civil Engineer. However, he soon realized that writing was his true calling. As a result, he took a leap and never looked back.

No sci-fi show or movie actively tries to predict the future. However, more often than not, some of the best additions to the sci-fi genre tell stories that revolve around the potential long-term implications of present-world technologies. Owing to this, some of the best sci-fi TV shows end up foreseeing the threats and benefits of technology that we are increasingly growing dependent upon.

Jonathan Nolan's Person of Interest is a highly-acclaimed sci-fi thriller that premiered over a decade ago. Yet, its masterful exploration of everything from artificial intelligence to surveillance feels surprisingly relevant today. After rewatching the series in 2026, it is hard not to notice how it almost feels like a documentary.

In its long five-season runtime, CBS's Person of Interest does not strive to build Rome in one day. Instead, it initially disguises itself as any other procedural tech-thriller on network television. However, as it gradually progresses into its second season, it expands its vision and becomes incredibly ambitious with its almost prophetic story beats.

Person Of Interest Feels More Like A Cautionary Documentary In 2026

MovieStills DB

Reminiscent of movies like Minority Report and anime like Psycho-Pass, Person of Interest introduces a computer program called "the Machine." The program in question is able to crunch mass surveillance data and predict crimes before they happen. This makes it a useful tool for the federal government.

While "the Machine" in Person of Interest still remains in the realm of fiction, modern AI surveillance software is becoming increasingly sophisticated and invasive. Like the Jonathan Nolan show, it even raises questions surrounding whether it is justified to sacrifice individual privacy and civil liberties at the expense of serving the perceived "greater good."

Person of Interest later introduces a rogue A.I. called Samaritan. It is nothing like the mainstream evil artificial intelligence from movies like Terminator. Instead, it functions more as a pervasive surveillance state that pulls many threads from the behind the scenes. It delays traffic lights to keep political opponents stuck in traffic, manipulates search engines, and even alters news headlines to change public opinion.

In 2026, internet algorithms are largely driven by AI-generated content. Search engines, too, are actively promoting AI, allowing skewed algorithms and machine-generated noise to control everything from consumer choices to voting decisions. As depicted in the show, mega-corporations, too, have grown so much in power that even governments can no longer regulate them.

One Episode In Person Of Interest Seems Chillingly Prophetic

Image via MovieStillsDB

In one of its most compelling episodes from season 1, titled "No Good Deed," Person of Interest walks through the story of an NSA analyst named Henry Peck. Henry is portrayed as a regular paper-pusher who notices how quickly the government processes copious amounts of data in a short duration. This helps him deduce that a secret, mass-surveillance machine exists.

When he tries to learn more, he is labeled as a traitor and even assassins are sent to kill him. His story ends with him being forced to go into hiding forever only because he uncovered the government's secret surveillance network.

Almost a year after this episode aired for the first time, Edward Snowden discovered almost the exact same bulk-data programs at the NSA in 2013. Like Henry, he, too, was forced to flee to escape government prosecution after he leaked the documents.

With this prophetic real-world parallel, the Jonathan Nolan sci-fi series proved that Oscar Wilde was right on the money when he said, "Life imitates Art far more than Art imitates Life."

In one of its most compelling episodes from season 1, titled "No Good Deed," Person of Interest walks through the story of an NSA analyst named Henry Peck. Henry is portrayed as a regular paper-pusher who notices how quickly the government processes copious amounts of data in a short duration. items.author: andy.chalk@pcgamer.com (Andy Chalk)
items.summary: BioWare was a legendary studio, and its shocking closure today has inspired numerous tributes from fans and fellow game developers alike. One of the most
items.text:
BioWare was a legendary studio, and its shocking closure today has inspired numerous tributes from fans and fellow game developers alike. One of the most notable came from CD Projekt joint CEO Michał Nowakowski, who credited the studio for the big role it played in bringing The Witcher to life.

It's hard to overstate the impact BioWare had on computer RPGs, from effectively resurrecting the genre in the 1990s with Baldur's Gate through the creation of Neverwinter Nights, Knights of the Old Republic, Dragon Age, and Mass Effect. But less well known, outside of RPG fan circles at least, is that its influence goes far beyond that. CD Projekt, which is arguably the contemporary equivalent of BioWare, literally got started with BioWare games.

The relationship began when CD Projekt approached BioWare and Interplay about localizing Baldur's Gate for Poland; it got the gig, and the Polish release became a major hit. A subsequent deal to localize Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance fell apart when Interplay did, but CD Projekt's relationship with BioWare held firm.

"Bioware has been a massive part of CDPR history," Nowakowski wrote on X. "We befriended them when localizing and selling Baldur’s Gate games in Poland, Czech, and Slovakia. And later they were great help when lending us their engine for Witcher 1, sharing their wisdom and even giving us a spot at their booth at E3."

Bioware has been a massive part of CDPR history. We befriended them when localizing and selling Baldur’s Gate games in Poland, Czech, and Slovakia. And later they were great help when lending us their engine for Witcher 1, sharing their wisdom and even giving us a spot at their booth at E3. I had a pleasure to visit them a few times in Edmonton and also host them in our Warsaw office. Very sad for the people affected, but also sad to see a legendary brand go down. Not a great day in the games industry.October 21, 2026

That was the Aurora Engine, BioWare's followup to the Infinity Engine, and was used for Neverwinter Nights, Knights of the Old Republic, Jade Empire, and as Nowakowski said, The Witcher, the RPG that introduced CD Projekt to the world and market the beginning of its journey to game industry powerhouse. In a 2014 interview with Polygon, CD Projekt co-founder Marcin Iwinski talked about the studio's early days working with BioWare and Interplay, and how it moved quickly to work on The Witcher after that Baldur's Gate: Dark Alliance fell through: "It all started, in a way, with Baldur's Gate."

And BioWare did in fact share space with CD Projekt at E3, giving the studio a chance to show its new RPG to the world: Ryszard Chojnowski, a translator and localizer whose credits include both The Witcher and Baldur's Gate 2, shared a pair of photos showing CD Projekt's corner of BioWare's booth at E3 2004:

A tu jeszcze jedno wspomnienie.m z BioWare. Rok 2004 i po raz pierwszy pokazujemy Wiedźmina na ich stoisku. Mamy oddzielone kotarą miejsce z komputerem, na którym działa jako tako demo na silniku Aurora https://t.co/SH8FKQF9zuOctober 21, 2026

Nowakowski concluded, "I had a pleasure to visit them a few times in Edmonton and also host them in our Warsaw office. Very sad for the people affected, but also sad to see a legendary brand go down. Not a great day in the games industry."

Not a great day indeed.

items.title: Modern Warfare 4 players declare 'broken' on DMZ perk that lets you self-revive after full death
items.author: Morgan Park
items.summary: Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's big extraction mode DMZ has been out for one day, so it's a bit early to make sweeping declarations about balance, but even
items.text:
Call of Duty: Modern Warfare 4's big extraction mode DMZ has been out for one day, so it's a bit early to make sweeping declarations about balance, but even I'm raising an eyebrow at an operator trait that the internet is already calling broken.

That's "broken" in the "so overpowered it shouldn't exist" way, not the "literally doesn't work way," though when you see Possum in action, it does give the impression of a bug.

Possum: Allows a self revive into last stand from death, storing health to maximum, once per match (Image credit: Activision Blizzard)As someone who's been around the extraction shooter block, it's a very powerful trump card. It doesn't take that long to get, either: If you beeline straight to it on the Warfighter skill tree, you can do it in a handful of matches.

To be clear, this is not the same as reviving yourself during the DBNO (down but not out) state, which anyone can do from level 1: Possum means you can be a cold, dead, lootable body, and then suddenly spring back to life.

I'm not surprised folks are panicky about the prospect of playing around lobbies full of Possum players. There's already one clip circulating (per xFleXy_ on X) of someone fully killing a player, turning their back to fight other nearby enemies, then getting shot in the back by the guy they just killed.

Umm I kill & finish the guy in the white skin and then he suddenly pops up and kills me??? @InfinityWard @CallofDutyCM https://t.co/XFrgD6MRCIOctober 20, 2026

That's the nightmare scenario, though the perk has drawbacks that xFleXy could've exploited if they'd known Possum existed. The self-revive isn't quick, and once it's done they still have to pick themselves up from DBNO with a tourniquet. If the killer is paying attention when that first step happens, they can easily end them for good before they stand back up.

I reckon Infinity Ward didn't envision folks using the perk to instantly turn the table on a lost fight. Per the name, you're likely meant to sit still, play dead, then self-revive after your corpse has been picked clean and the killers have moved on. You lose some stuff, but you escape with your operator (which can be expensive to replace). Call of Duty YouTuber JGOD demonstrated this use case in his own video.

1st time using the Possum Trait in DMZ🟢Waited 3 minutes for the players to move on🟢They dropped a 2 plate while looting my Free Kit🟢Then Exfilled https://t.co/SHFgd2gJv1October 21, 2026

In those terms, a trait like Possum is a great fit for DMZ, which is designed not to be as punishing as other extraction shooters. The problem is its execution: Players who just won a fight should not always have to worry that their victim is going to stand back up and kill them. Maybe using Possum should make more noise in the moment, or require a long wait (like 5 to 10 minutes) to use. Infinity Ward needs to underline how bad of an idea it is to use while enemies are around, or in lieu of that, players need a way to burn bodies.

Possum seems very OP in PvP fights. from r/DMZ

"Burn bodies," in this context, refers to Hunt: Showdown, the other extraction shooter with this exact ability. That game's Possum, called Necromancer, works the same way, except that others have the option to set your corpse on fire and wait for a sound cue that confirms "this guy ain't getting up." It's a great bit of balance, because it puts the onus on the killer to already have a molotov cocktail on-hand, look for another way to start a fire, or leave your corpse and accept you may come back. Sometimes Necromancer saves your bacon, sometimes not.

Whatever the eventual solution is, I expect Infinity Ward to react soon.

items.title: The One Thing EA Has Always Been Good At Is Killing Video Game Studios
items.author: Zack Zwiezen
items.summary: On Wednesday, Electronic Arts announced it was closing beloved RPG studio BioWare and canceling an in-development Mass Effect sequel. It’s a reminder that,
items.text:
On Wednesday, Electronic Arts announced it was closing beloved RPG studio BioWare and canceling an in-development Mass Effect sequel. It’s a reminder that, despite EA being owned by new people, the company’s long-running tradition of buying and closing down game studios and publishers, often after gutting them and treating them poorly for years before dealing the final blow, will continue.

Since its founding in 1982, Electronic Arts (the winner of the “Worst Company in America” award in 2012 and 2013) has only really done one thing consistently. Releasing and publishing successful, popular video games? Nope. Making good decisions or protecting its employees? Nah. It’s rarely been consistent at doing any of that stuff. The one thing EA seems capable of doing regardless of the year or the people in charge is buying and then closing studios. It is really good at doing that. It’s probably the best company in the game industry at buying and then killing studios like horrific clockwork.

Just five years after EA was created, it bought and then quickly shut down its first game company. And since then, it has continued to acquire and kill studios regularly. It’s like a bored and spoiled rich kid asking for new toys, only to toss them aside for the help to throw away as it focuses on something shiny and new. People might lose their jobs, but there are profits to be earned and numbers to go up, you see.

Here’s a list of all the studios, developers, and publishers EA has chewed up and spit into the garbage over the decades:

Batteries Included – Purchased in 1987 and closed that same year.

Origin Systems – Purchased in 1992. Closed in 2004.

Bullfrog Productions – Purchased in 1995. Closed in 2001.

Maxis – Purchased in 1997. Closed in 2015. (Studio name still used by EA.)

Westwood Studios / EA Pacific – Purchased in 1998. Closed in 2003.

Kesmai – Purchased in 1999. Closed in 2001.

DreamWorks Interactive / Danger Close Games – Purchased in 2000. Closed in 2013.

Black Box Games – Purchased in 2002. Closed in 2013.

NuFX / EA Chicago – Purchased in 2004. Closed in 2007.

Hypnotix – Purchased and shut down in 2005. Team folded into EA Tiburon.

Mythic Entertainment – Purchased in 2006. Closed in 2014.

Phenomic Game Development – Purchased in 2006. Closed in 2013.

Headgate Studios / EA Salt Lake – Purchased in 2006. Closed in 2017.

Pandemic Studios – Purchased in 2007. Closed in 2009.

J2MSoft – Purchased in 2008 and folded into EA Korea.

Playfish – Purchased in 2009. Closed in 2013.

Chillingo – Purchased in 2010. Began shutting down in 2017. Fully closed in 2023.

Industrial Toys – Purchased in 2018. Closed in 2023.

BioWare – Purchased in 2007. Closed in 2026.

Looking at the list above, it seems like EA is more interested in destroying the game industry than making video games people will like and buy. It’s easier to explain a lot of EA’s decisions as the company trying to burn the whole house down instead of the much harder-to-buy idea that EA is actually trying to be a successful publisher people like.

By my count, BioWare is the 19th studio or game publisher EA has acquired and killed since 1987. But it’s tricky to nail that number down as EA moves people around, folds teams into other teams, and quietly reshuffles parts of the company. For example, Maxis (the studio behind SimCity) is still technically around, but in name only, as the original Maxis was shut down in 2015. Fun fact: when EA killed Batteries Included in 1987, it did something similar. The more things change…

I’d love to say that EA has learned its lesson and, moving forward, it won’t keep doing this song and dance. But with EA going private and being owned by the worst blunt rotation of people you can imagine, I’m not convinced it won’t keep doing this. In fact, it’s probably going to get worse. Welcome to the modern video game industry. It’s completely on fire, and the people with money don’t seem to care.

items.title: 35 English Loanwords That Come From the Japanese Language
items.author: Coto Academy Staff Writer
items.summary: While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly
items.text:
While Japanese has tons of English loanwords, English actually borrows quite a bit from Japanese as well. Words like sushi, karate, or tsunami are so commonly used that it might be easy to forget that they’re loanwords from Japan.

Let’s discover some common Japanese loanwords in English, covering some of the old and some of the new, but this blog is by no means exhaustive. By the end of this article, who knows? New words are probably being borrowed at this very moment.

Why Do Japanese and English Borrow so Many Words From Each Other?

Since Japanese and English come from very different places with distinct cultures, cuisines, and geographic characteristics or phenomena, the more exposed we are to each other’s cultures, the more new concepts and words we encounter. It makes sense that English would just adopt the words for Japanese food items like “sushi” or “ramen.”

However, the word tsunami is also of Japanese origin. It just so happens that English had no word for huge tidal waves, so it borrowed tsunami from Japanese. Often when a word sufficiently describes something we don’t have a word for, we just adopt it into our language. As you are probably well aware, Japanese quite often does the same.

You’ve probably experienced what could be called the katakana glitch. You see a katakana word, and you just can’t figure out what it is until you mouth it, then you finally figure out that biiru (ビール) is actually “beer”. You probably can think of many more English loanwords in Japanese, such as soccer, or sakkaa (サッカー), and even modern slang like rizz, or rizu (リズ). New words are crossing over, perhaps because the internet and pop culture spread new trends faster than ever before.

Note that this doesn’t always happen; when baseball was introduced to Japan, they made their own word for the sport, yakyuu (野球), which is made up of the words field, or 野 (ya), and ball, 球 (kyuu).

Japanese Loanwords Used in English for Food and Entertainment

In 2013, UNESCO named Japanese food an intangible cultural heritage. The flavors and practices associated with Japanese food are unique. Many of the Japanese loanwords in English reflect that uniqueness. Ikigai, as a concept, has been making waves in the English-speaking world in recent years. Iki means life and gai means value, so the term translates to ‘reason for being’. The idea is that with a reason for being or a purpose, people can live more fulfilling lives, as those lives get longer.
31. Tsunami (津波)

Originating from harbor (tsu) and wave (nami), this word has been in use in many unfortunate circumstances recently. As with the original Japanese, it describes a large sea wave caused by an earthquake. Tsunami has also been used in a figurative sense to mean a large and sudden amount of something.
32. Samurai (侍)

Many words from Japanese history are usually adopted directly into English, and samurai is no exception. Samurai describes a specific warrior class that only existed in the context of Japan. Calling them “Japanese knights” just wouldn’t capture what they were and the place they had in Japanese society.
Likewise, many other historical Japanese terms for different social positions or figures, like shogun, daimyo, or even ninja, are simply borrowed in English.
33. Katana (刀)

While katana actually just means “sword,” in English it has come to refer to the specific Japanese sword with its characteristic curved blade that was used by the samurai. Likely due to its unique aesthetics, carefully crafted by skilled blacksmiths, it caught the attention of foreigners. Thus, now we use the word katana to describe the iconic sword from Japan.
34. Kimono (着物)

The kimono is a beautiful, elegant garment that has come to be known as the national dress of Japan. So, there’s no question why English adopted the word kimono to describe this iconic piece of clothing. There isn’t even an equivalent type of clothing to the kimono in English-speaking countries; while there are dresses and robes, none of them are quite a kimono.
35. Shinkansen (新幹線)

While English has the word “bullet train,” it’s not uncommon for people to opt to use the word “shinkansen” instead. Japan’s efficient transportation system, particularly the bullet train, has become such an image of the nation that shinkansen is now widely known in English. Often when people visit Japan, they might say they want to ride the “shinkansen” rather than the “bullet train.”
Conclusion:

You might be surprised how many words the English language adopts from Japanese alone. You’ve no doubt been using many of them and as the English language continues to borrow words from Japanese, you’ll end up using even more Japanese, in English. The truth is, languages constantly borrow from each other, showing how we exchange ideas all the time.
As a matter of fact, Japanese doesn’t just borrow words from English. To find out more, read our blog: Loan Words in Japanese that Don’t Come from English!
Want to study Japanese with a native teacher?

If you want to learn more about the Japanese language, why not consider studying Japanese at Coto Academy? If you can’t make it to Japan yet, an online course is one of the best ways to start your Japanese language journey. Coto Academy offers a comprehensive Japanese course that’s available online, in Tokyo or Yokohama! Get a free consultation and join our class today!
Contact us for more information and make sure to follow our blog for more insight into the Japanese language, culture and society.
Does English have Japanese loanwords?

Yes, English language borrows a lot of Japanese words. For example, tsunami, tycoon and sudoku came from the Japanese equivalent. English language also retains a lot of original Japanese food-related words, like sushi, katsu and dashi.
What English words are borrowed from Japan?
Among many of them, the most common English words borrowed from Japan are:
Tsunami
Karaoke
Tycoon
Sushi
Skosh
Ramen
Futon
Does Japan borrow words from the English language?
Yes, Japanese has around 4,500 words that are borrowed from English. Loanwords borrowed from a foreign language is called gairaigo (外来語).
Tsunami

Ramen

items.author: Coto Academy Teachers

items.text:
Welcome to Japan! Along with your first steps in your new life in Tokyo, one of your first priorities is to start learning Japanese. Some of you might already have a certain level of Japanese ability, such as reading and writing hiragana and katakana. But what if you have never learned Japanese before?

When you have completely zero knowledge of Japanese, we recommend you join what is called a Japanese Crash Course, like ones offered at Coto Academy. In 4 weeks, you will learn the fundamentals of Japanese, directly useful for your daily life, including an introduction to hiragana and katakana.

Interested in joining our Japanese Crash Course, or wondering if it’s the right fit for you? We’d love to help! Simply fill out the contact form below, and our English-speaking staff will get back to you shortly.


Get In Touch With Our Team!


What is Japanese Crash Course?

Coto Academy’s Japanese Crash Course is an intensive, short-term survival program designed specifically for complete beginners and new residents in Japan who need to build functional, everyday Japanese skills as quickly as possible.

AspectDetails

Target LevelZero Beginner (No prior Japanese knowledge required)

Duration1 to 4 weeks (standard core unit runs 4 weeks)

SchedulePart-time intensive (e.g., 4 days/week, 2 hours/day)

LocationsCoto Academy locations (such as Azabu, Iidabashi, Yokohama) & Online

Key Features & Learning Focus


Practical, Conversation-First Curriculum: Focuses on immediate, practical communication rather than heavy grammar theory. Students master key phrases across 9 real-life scenarios, including ordering at restaurants, shopping, asking for directions, self-introductions, and simple daily interactions.

Basic Literacy: Teaches Hiragana and Katakana reading and writing, alongside common Kanji frequently encountered in daily life (such as street signs, menus, and shop notices).

Small Class Sizes: Limited to a maximum of 8 students per class (averaging 3–6), ensuring maximum speaking time and individual feedback from instructors.

Experiential Learning (Tokyo Explorer): Includes interactive outdoor activities where students put their classroom learning to the test in real-world settings like local cafes, supermarkets, and izakayas.


How is Japanese Crash Course Different From Beginner Japanese Lessons?

Japanese Crash Course is a special course designed for individuals who have completely zero knowledge or prior experience in learning Japanese. On the other hand, some beginner Japanese lessons might already expect students to know about basic hiragana and katakana and phrases.

It is important to clarify with your chosen Japanese language school if the beginner lessons they offer are designed for total beginners or not.

Who is This Japanese Crash Course For?

Other than for total beginners, we think Japanese Crash Course is the right fit for you if you:

1. New Arrivals Who Want Practical, Everyday Japanese

If you just arrived in Japan and need to start communicating right away, this course prioritizes real-life interaction over dry theory. Rather than spending weeks on abstract grammar rules, you learn functional phrases you can use immediately for shopping, ordering food, and navigating daily life. The speaking-first approach gets you talking from day one so you feel confident handling everyday tasks.

2. Returning Learners Rebuilding Their Foundation

If you studied Japanese before but took a long break, this course serves as an efficient refresher. It helps you clean up forgotten grammar, review Hiragana and Katakana, and fix gaps in your foundational skills. This reactivates your speaking momentum without forcing you into an overly advanced class.

3. Short-Term Visitors, Tourists & Travelers

If you are visiting Japan for a few weeks or months, you can enjoy a flexible language immersion experience without long-term commitments. Unlike traditional language schools that require 6-month or 1-year visa commitments, you can enroll for short blocks starting from just 1 week. It offers a hands-on way to make your trip richer by learning the language while exploring the country.

What’s The Experiential Learning at Coto Academy’s Japanese Crash Course?

At Coto Academy, we believe learning a language shouldn’t feel like studying for a history exam. Japanese is a living, breathing tool, and you should get to use it from day one!

That’s where Experiential Learning comes in. Once a week, we take the learning outside! Guided by your teacher, you’ll head out of our campus to complete fun missions like ordering a customized drink, asking a shopkeeper for recommendations, or getting directions to a nearby landmark.

Inside the class, you can expect role-plays like introducing yourself to new friends and handling shopping questions.

Ready to Start Your Japanese Journey?

If you’re excited to learn Japanese by actually living it, our Japanese Crash Course is ready for you! Classes run in small groups to make sure everyone gets plenty of speaking time and personal guidance.

Come join us, meet fellow learners from around the world, and start exploring Japan with confidence!


Contact Us and Start Learning Japanese!


FAQ

Do I need any prior Japanese knowledge to join this course?

No prior experience is necessary! The Japanese Crash Course is specially designed for absolute beginners (Zero Beginner). Whether you haven’t learned a single word yet or only know konnichiwa, our native teachers will walk you through daily essential phrases, as well as hiragana and katakana, step by step.

How long does the course last, and how flexible is the schedule?

We offer high flexibility so you don’t need to make a long-term commitment. While the core unit runs for 4 weeks, you can enroll for anywhere from 1 week to 12 weeks depending on your availability and length of stay in Japan. Classes typically run part-time multiple days a week, making it easy to fit into a busy schedule.

What is the class size like?

To ensure everyone gets personal attention and plenty of speaking time, our classes are kept strictly small, with a maximum of 8 students per class (averaging around 3 to 6 students). You will have continuous opportunities to practice active conversation rather than just passively listening to a lecture.

items.title: How to Make a Phone Call in Japanese Beyond Moshi Moshi
items.author: Lopez Esai
items.summary: When you’re in Japan, there are cases where you might need to make a phone call in Japanese, whether that’s for making a restaurant reservation, calling for
items.text:
When you’re in Japan, there are cases where you might need to make a phone call in Japanese, whether that’s for making a restaurant reservation, calling for an emergency, or checking on your friend. Here is where you can no longer rely on gestures or reading subtle body language to figure out what the other person is saying. It’s a true test of your Japanese listening comprehension and speaking skills, where you need to respond rather quickly and hold a conversation with just words and phrases you know.

Contrary to popular belief, you should not use moshi moshi all the time. So, let’s break down how phone calls work in Japanese and how you can navigate them with ease and confidence!

A Bit of Japanese Phone Call Etiquette

Japan is known for its polite and sometimes complex etiquette, which can change depending on the level of formality, and this can apply to phone calls. Whenever you answer a call from a business or service, as a general rule, you use polite language, like the です/ます form. When making calls for work, like when speaking to a client or customer, you should always use keigo, formal Japanese conjugations.

So, a big question you might be asking is whether or not you should use もしもし (moshi moshi). This expression is commonly used when answering phone calls between friends, family, and people you’re more comfortable with. You wouldn’t really use もしもし in formal situations like when talking to strangers, service staff, or on work calls.

Japanese phone etiquette is not complicated and generally follows similar patterns of politeness you would observe in English or your native tongue. You should always start the call with a polite greeting and end with a polite expression conveying farewell or appreciation. So, let’s go through how to navigate a call completely in Japanese, step-by-step.

Making Phone Calls in Japanese

The way you make phone calls in Japanese varies depending on whether you are answering or initiating the call, and whether you’re in a formal or casual context. So, let’s go through some common situations where you would be calling in formal contexts (for work and speaking with clients), casual contexts (talking to friends, family, or people you know), and when speaking to services, like making a reservation.

Making Formal Phone Calls in Japanese

When making formal calls, you must always use very polite Japanese, which, of course, starts with a very respectful greeting. Depending on whether you’ve worked with the person you’re calling before or you are calling someone for the first time, the greeting will actually change.

1. Greeting Business Partners or People You Work with Often

Similar to writing business emails in Japanese, the most common formal greeting in phone calls is お世話になっております (Osewa ni natte orimasu) followed by your name and company. You usually use this greeting with people you have worked with in the past.

Example:

お世話になっております。株式会社アイスクリームのロイです。
Osewa ni natte orimasu. Kabushiki geisha aisu kuriimu no roi desu.
Thank you for your constant support. This is Roy from Ice Cream Inc.

However, if you’re calling a colleague, you should use the phrase お疲れ様です (otsukaresama desu). It doesn’t have a great English equivalent, but it conveys appreciation for your colleagues’ hard work and is often used as a greeting to fellow co-workers, including on phone calls. Note: you wouldn’t say お世話になっております to colleagues on phone calls.

Example:

お疲れ様です。ロイです。
Otsukaresama desu. Roi desu.
Hello, this is Roy.

2. Greeting Clients or People You Haven’t Met

When it comes to calling clients, customers, or people you just met, you will usually use a greeting that conveys appreciation. You usually thank the person for answering the call with the expression お電話ありがとうございます (odenwa arigatou gozaimasu), meaning “thank you for the call.”

Example:

お電話ありがとうございます。株式会社アイスクリームのロイでございます。
Odenwa arigatou gozaimasu. Kabushiki gaisha aisu kuriimu no roi degozaimasu.
Thank you very much for letting me call. This is Roy from Ice Cream Inc.

3. Answering Phone Calls in Formal Situations

When answering a phone call in a business or work capacity, you use extra-polite language known as humble and honorific forms. So, when you receive a call, it’s common to say はい、〜です (hai, ~ desu), meaning “yes, this is…” This is a very polite way to answer a call while also immediately introducing yourself so the caller knows who they are speaking to.

Example:

はい、ロイです。
Hai, roi desu.
Yes, this is Roy speaking.

To make the phrase even more formal, you can change です to its humble form: 〜でございます (degozaimasu). This phrase is very common when answering the phone in work situations.

Example:

はい、株式会社アイスクリームのロイでございます。
Hai, kabushiki gaisha aisu kuriimu no roi degozaimasu.
Hello, this is Roy speaking from Ice Cream Inc.

So, after the caller introduces themselves, if you’re receiving a call from a client company, even if you don’t know the caller directly, you can follow up with the phrase お世話になっております (osewa ni natte orimasu).

4. Asking to Talk to Someone Else

It’s quite common when you’re trying to contact somebody on their work phone number that you will end up calling a department desk, which directs the call to whoever is available. So, if you want to get in contact with a specific person, here is how you can do that.

Example:

すみません、山田さんがいらっしゃいますでしょうか？話させて頂いてよろしいでしょうか？
Sumimasen, Yamada-san ga irashaimasudeshouka? Hanasasete itadaite yoroshii deshouka?
Excuse me, is Yamada-san available? May I speak with him?

5. Scheduling a Meeting

Scheduling a meeting is one of the most common reasons to make a formal phone call in Japanese. Since you’re asking for someone’s valuable time, you’ll want to use polite, humble language to make your request sound considerate and professional.

A common, professional phrase for “meeting” or “discussion” is 打ち合わせ (uchiawase). It’s the everyday business word for a meeting with a client or colleague, and it’s often written with the honorific prefix お to become お打ち合わせ (o-uchiawase) when talking about the other person’s time. 日程 (nittei) means “schedule” or “dates,” and 調整 (chousei) means “to adjust” or “to arrange.” Together with させていただきたいのですが, a humble way of saying “I would like to,” the phrase softly opens the conversation without sounding demanding.

Example:

お打ち合わせの日程を調整させていただきたいのですが、ご都合のよろしい日はございますか？
O uchiawase no nittei o chousei sasete itadakitai no desu ga, gotsugou no yoroshii hi wa gozaimasu ka?
I would like to arrange a time for us to meet. Is there a day that works well for you?

6. When You Can’t Hear the Other Person

Call reception often varies, so it can be hard to hear people. How do you communicate respectfully that you can’t hear someone you’re on the phone with? You can always use one of the most useful Japanese phrases: もう一度お願いします (mou ichido onegaishimasu), which means “one more time, please.” It works as a respectful way to ask someone to repeat themselves for both in-person and over-the-phone interactions.

Example:

すみません、もう一度お願いします。
Sumimasen, mou ichido onegaishimasu.
Excuse me, can you say it one more time, please?

If you want to ask someone if they can hear you, the phrase 聞こえますか？ (kikoe masuka?) works perfectly for this. On business calls, to amp up the politeness, you can say 聞こえますでしょうか？ (kikou masudeshouka?). Adding でしょうか？ (deshouka?) softens the whole expression and works well when you want to show greater respect.

Example:

すみません、聞こえますでしょうか？
Sumimasen, kikoemasu deshouka?
Excuse me, are you able to hear me?

7. Saying Farewell in Formal Calls

Whenever you’re talking with someone who isn’t your family or friends, whether it’s for work, to inquire about a service, or talk to a teacher or coach, you almost always end the call with 失礼します (shitsureishimasu).

It literally means “I’m being rude”. But despite its apologetic nuance, it’s used as a polite way to say goodbye, kind of like saying I’m sorry for hanging up.” You usually say it right before you or the person you’re speaking to ends the call.

Example:

失礼します。
Shitsurei shimasu.
Goodbye.

In formal work calls, it’s common to end the call with a polite expression that conveys a sense of appreciation and desire to work together again. よろしくお願いします (Yoroshiku Onegaishimasu) is one of the most common phrases you can use to end a formal call.

Example:

よろしくお願いします。失礼します。
Yoroshiku onegaishimasu. Shitsureishimasu.
I look forward to working/speaking with you again. Goodbye.

When responding to よろしくお願いします (yoroshiku onegaishimasu), it’s very common to say こちらこそよろしくお願いします (kochira koso yoroshiku onegaishimasu), meaning “No, I’m the one who is looking forward to working with you again”. The phrase こちらこそ (kochira koso) is great for expressing a sense of humility and respect for the one other person by putting the responsibility or appreciation on your side.

Making Phone Calls To Friends, Family, and People You Know

When calling friends, family, and people you know, you can drop some of the formalities and use more casual language. But similar to formal calls, greetings tend to change when answering or initiating a phone call. So, let’s break down how to make phone calls in a more casual context.

8. Answering or Starting a Call

もしもし (moshi moshi) is the classic phone greeting in Japanese, and you’ll use it with friends, family, and people you’re comfortable with. It works much like “hello?” in English, and you can use it both when you answer a call and when you start one. It’s also handy if the connection is bad and you want to check that the other person can still hear you.

When answering a call from someone you know, you can simply say もしもし, or add a bit more, like their name or a quick “hey.” If you’re the one calling, it’s polite to say who you are right after.

Example:

もしもし、ケンです。今、大丈夫？
Moshi moshi, Ken desu. Ima, daijoubu?
Hello, it’s Ken. Is now a good time?

Keep in mind that you’d skip もしもし on formal or work calls, where you’d use the greetings from the previous section instead.

9. Checking if They Have Time to Talk

Even in casual calls, it’s good manners to check whether the other person is free before you jump into your reason for calling. Calls can interrupt someone on a train, at work, or in the middle of dinner, so a quick check shows consideration. 今 (ima) means “now,” and 大丈夫 (daijoubu) means “okay” or “alright,” so together they ask “is now okay?”

With people you’re closer with, you can keep it short. With someone a bit older or less familiar, add です/ます to keep things polite.

Example:

もしもし、今ちょっと話せる？
Moshi moshi, ima chotto hanaseru?
Hello, can you talk for a bit right now?

Example 2:

今、お時間大丈夫ですか？
Ima, ojikan daijoubu desu ka?
Do you have a moment right now?

If the other person is busy, you might hear them say 今ちょっと無理 (ima chotto muri), meaning “I can’t right now,” or 後でかけ直すね (ato de kakenaosu ne), meaning “I’ll call you back later.” This is a good phrase to recognize since it’s very common.

10. Making Plans With Friends

One of the most common reasons to call a friend is to make plans, whether it’s grabbing food, going to a movie, or just hanging out. In casual Japanese, the easiest way to invite someone is by using the negative question form 〜しない？ (~shinai?), which literally asks “won’t you ~?” but is actually a friendly way of saying “want to ~?” It sounds much softer and more natural than a direct question.

For more casual invitations, you can also use the volitional form 〜しよう (~shiyou), meaning “let’s ~.”

Example:

今週末、ご飯食べに行かない？
Konshuu matsu, gohan tabe ni ikanai?
Want to go eat this weekend?

Example 2:

じゃあ、土曜日の夜に渋谷で会おう！
Jaa, doyoubi no yoru ni Shibuya de aou!
Then, let’s meet in Shibuya on Saturday night!

If they say yes, you might hear うん、いいね！ (un, ii ne!), meaning “yeah, sounds good!” If they’re not free, they may say ごめん、その日は予定がある (gomen, sono hi wa yotei ga aru), meaning “sorry, I have plans that day.”

11. Ending a Casual Call

Just like in formal calls, you’ll want to end the conversation politely. The difference is that casual goodbyes are much shorter and more relaxed. また (mata) means “again,” and ね (ne) adds a friendly tone, so またね literally means “see you again!” You can also say じゃあね (jaa ne), another very common way to say “bye for now” among friends.

Before hanging up, it’s common to thank them for their time or confirm your plans one more time.

Example:

じゃあ、また明日ね！
Jaa, mata ashita ne!
Well then, see you tomorrow!

Example 2:

電話ありがとう！またね。
Denwa arigatou! Mata ne.
Thanks for calling! Talk to you later.

If you’re talking to someone a bit older or more distant, you can swap in a more polite option like 失礼します (shitsurei shimasu), which is the standard way to end a call politely, or ありがとうございました (arigatou gozaimashita).

Making Phone Calls to Service Staff in Japanese

Phone calls to service staff are more formal than calls to friends or family, but you don’t need to employ the same level of keigo when making calls at work. You also don’t really need to say formal greetings, since the service staff will immediately introduce themselves and ask how they can help you. So, all you really need to do is go straight to the point and respond.

12. Calling to Make a Reservation

Making a reservation in Japanese on the phone is relatively straightforward. You just state you’re calling to make a reservation and then the staff will ask follow-up questions to get your name under which the reservation will be made, the number of people, and time. Let’s take a look at a general phone call to make a reservation.
Example:

(You dial the restaurant number to call)

スタッフ：お電話ありがとうございます。ベストタコスです。
Sutaffu: Odenwa arigatou gozaimasu. Besuto Takosu desu.
Staff: Thank you for calling. This is Best Tacos.

あなた：すみません、今日の午後9時に5人で予約をしたいのですが。
Anata: Sumimasen, kyou no gogo kuji ni gonin de yoyaku o shitai no desu ga.
You: Excuse me, I would like to make a reservation for 5 people at 9 p.m. today.

スタッフ：本日9時に5名様でご予約でよろしいでしょうか？お席を確認いたしますので、少々お待ちください。
Sutaffu: Honjitsu kuji ni gomeisama de goyoyaku de yoroshii deshouka? Oseki o kakunin itashimasu node, shoushou omachi kudasai.
Staff: A reservation for 5 people at 9 p.m. today, correct? Please wait a moment while I check if seats are available.

あなた：はい、お願いします。
Anata: Hai, onegaishimasu.
You: Yes, please.

スタッフ：お待たせしました。お席をご用意できます。お名前とお電話番号をお伺いしてもよろしいでしょうか？
Sutaffu: Omatase shimashita. Oseki o goyoui dekimasu. Onamae to odenwa bangou o oukagai shitemo yoroshii deshouka?
Staff: Thank you for waiting. We can prepare a table for you. May I have your name and phone number?

あなた：ロイと申します。電話番号は090-1234-5678です。
Anata: Roi to moushimasu. Denwa bangou wa zero kyuu zero no ichi ni san yon no go roku nana hachi desu.
You: My name is Roy. My phone number is 090-1234-5678.

スタッフ：ご予約ありがとうございます。ロイ様、9時に5名様でお待ちしております。
Sutaffu: Goyoyaku arigatou gozaimasu. Roi-sama, kuji ni gomeisama de omachi shite orimasu.
Staff: Thank you for your reservation. Roy, we look forward to seeing your party of 5 at 9 p.m.

あなた：ありがとうございます。失礼します。
Anata: Arigatou gozaimasu. Shitsurei shimasu.
You: Thank you. Goodbye.

スタッフ：失礼いたします。
Sutaffu: Shitsurei itashimasu.
Staff: Goodbye.

13. Calling for a Delivery

One of the most common reasons you may need to call a service person is to reschedule a delivery. Usually, when you miss a delivery, you will find a notice slip in your mailbox with the phrase 再配達 (saihaitatsu), which means “redelivery.” Many companies also let you request it through an app or website.

On the slip or website, you will also find your package’s お問い合わせ番号 (Otoiawase bangou), which translates to “inquiry number.” There’s usually a phone number on the slip or website, and when you call it, the staff will ask for the inquiry number so they can easily identify your package and proceed with redelivering it.

So, here is how you can call the delivery company or driver to redeliver a package.

Example:

(You call the delivery company to reschedule a missed delivery)

スタッフ：お電話ありがとうございます。ジャパン宅配でございます。
Sutaffu: Odenwa arigatou gozaimasu. Japan Takuhai de gozaimasu.
Staff: Thank you for calling. This is Japan Delivery.

あなた：お世話になっております。荷物の再配達をお願いしたいのですが。
Anata: Osewa ni natte orimasu. Nimotsu no saihaitatsu o onegai shitai no desu ga.
You: Thank you for your support. I would like to request a redelivery of a package.

スタッフ：かしこまりました。お問い合わせ番号をお伺いしてもよろしいでしょうか？
Sutaffu: Kashikomarimashita. Otoiawase bangou o oukagai shitemo yoroshii deshouka?
Staff: Certainly. May I have your inquiry number?

あなた：はい、1234-5678-9012です。
Anata: Hai, ichi ni san yon no go roku nana hachi no kyuu zero ichi ni desu.
You: Yes, it’s 1234-5678-9012.

スタッフ：ありがとうございます。確認いたしますので、少々お待ちください。
Sutaffu: Arigatou gozaimasu. Kakunin itashimasu node, shoushou omachi kudasai.
Staff: Thank you. Please wait a moment while I check.

スタッフ：お待たせいたしました。ご希望のお届け時間はございますか？
Sutaffu: Omatase itashimashita. Gokibou no otodoke jikan wa gozaimasu ka?
Staff: Thank you for waiting. Do you have a preferred delivery time?

あなた：今日の夜7時から9時の間でお願いできますか？
Anata: Kyou no yoru shichiji kara kuji no aida de onegai dekimasu ka?
You: Could you deliver between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. tonight?

スタッフ：かしこまりました。本日19時から21時の間にお届けいたします。
Sutaffu: Kashikomarimashita. Honjitsu juukuji kara nijuuichiji no aida ni otodoke itashimasu.
Staff: Understood. We will deliver it between 7 p.m. and 9 p.m. today.

あなた：よろしくお願いします。失礼します。
Anata: Yoroshiku onegai shimasu. Shitsurei shimasu.
You: Thank you very much. Goodbye.

スタッフ：失礼いたします。
Sutaffu: Shitsurei itashimasu.
Staff: Goodbye.

But knowing just a few Japanese phrases can allow you to hold a phone call completely in Japanese, from making a reservation to making plans.
